title: Policy "Signed-in users can add documents" on public.documents does not tie written rows to their owner
description: Any signed-in user can create rows in other users' names in public.documents. Reproduced against a throwaway PostgreSQL database: 1 of the 9 attacks run on public.documents were let through (cross-insert).
root_cause: Policy "Signed-in users can add documents" does not check that owner_id is the caller when a row is written (insert).
intended_behavior: A signed-in user should read and change only rows whose owner_id is theirs, and the anonymous role (the public key) should have no access to rows of this table.

instructions: Create a throwaway PostgreSQL database with the Supabase roles (anon, authenticated, service_role) and auth.uid() reading request.jwt.claims, apply the migrations as a non-superuser, and insert one row for each of two synthetic users, A (alice@example.test) and B (bob@example.test). `proof-audit rls <migrations> --out <dir>` does this and records every probe in proofs.jsonl.

title: View public.invoice_summaries bypasses row level security
description: Anyone with your public anon key can read the rows behind public.invoice_summaries, and any signed-in user can read other users' rows through the view. Reproduced against a throwaway PostgreSQL database: 2 of the 2 attacks run on public.invoice_summaries were let through (view-read-anon, view-read-cross).
root_cause: The view runs with its owner's rights (it is not security_invoker), so the row level security on public.invoices is skipped when the view is read.
intended_behavior: A view over per-user rows should apply the caller's row level security (security_invoker), so each signed-in user sees only their own rows and the anonymous role sees none.

execution.attacker_perspective: Anyone with your public anon key can read rows of public.tickets, add rows to public.tickets, change rows in public.tickets and delete rows from public.tickets, and any signed-in user can read other users' rows, create rows in other users' names, create rows that belong to nobody, change other users' rows, delete other users' rows and give their own rows to another user.
instructions: Create a throwaway PostgreSQL database with the Supabase roles (anon, authenticated, service_role) and auth.uid() reading request.jwt.claims, apply the migrations as a non-superuser, and insert one row for each of two synthetic users, A (alice@example.test) and B (bob@example.test). `proof-audit rls <migrations> --out <dir>` does this and records every probe in proofs.jsonl.

In a transaction that you roll back afterwards, SET LOCAL ROLE and SET LOCAL request.jwt.claims as the anonymous caller (role anon), using the role and claims in the conditions, then run payload 1, 2, 3, 4.

In a transaction that you roll back afterwards, SET LOCAL ROLE and SET LOCAL request.jwt.claims as user A (role authenticated), using the role and claims in the conditions, then run payload 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10.
Replay the recorded probes with `proof-audit verify <dir>/proofs.jsonl`: it regenerates these statements from the migrations and compares the database's answers by content hash.

remediation.strategy: Drop or replace policy "Anyone can use tickets" on public.tickets with a condition that ties user_id to the caller (user_id = (select auth.uid())), and revoke the anon privileges the application does not need. Fix verified: 10 attacks now fail and 4 legitimate actions still work. The generated fix.sql section for public.tickets is attached as a starting point; review it before use.
